clinicalPearls: Typically follows a rapid acceleration-deceleration of the neck, most often a rear-end vehicle collision, straining the cervical soft tissues
Neck pain and stiffness often develop several hours to a day after the injury, along with headache and restricted movement
Whiplash-associated disorders are graded from no physical signs (grade 0) through musculoskeletal signs (grades I-II) to neurological signs (grade III) and fracture or dislocation (grade IV)
Apply a validated decision rule such as the Canadian C-spine rule to determine the need for imaging and to identify patients needing bony assessment
The priority in acute assessment is to exclude cervical fracture, dislocation, and spinal cord or nerve root injury
For uncomplicated injuries, early return to normal activity, reassurance, and active mobilisation give better outcomes than a collar and prolonged rest
Simple analgesia and exercise-based physiotherapy are the mainstays of management
Persistent pain, higher initial pain intensity, and psychological distress are associated with a slower recovery and chronic symptoms
Be alert to associated concussion, temporomandibular, or shoulder-girdle symptoms after the same injury
reference.pathophysiology: Whiplash results from sudden hyperextension followed by flexion (or the reverse) of the cervical spine during rapid acceleration-deceleration. This strains and may partially tear the cervical muscles, ligaments, facet joint capsules, and intervertebral discs, and can injure nerve roots or, in severe cases, cause fracture or cord injury. Peripheral tissue injury combined with central pain sensitisation and psychosocial factors contributes to chronic symptoms in some patients.
additionalDifferentials: Cervical spinal cord or nerve root injury
Shoulder girdle or temporomandibular joint injury
additionalInvestigations: Clinical clearance using the Canadian C-spine rule or NEXUS criteria before imaging
CT of the cervical spine for suspected fracture or in high-risk patients
MRI if there is neurological deficit, suspected cord or disc injury, or ligamentous instability
Plain radiographs where appropriate for lower-risk patients
CT or MR angiography if arterial dissection is suspected
redFlags: Neurological deficit, saddle or limb weakness, or signs of spinal cord injury
Midline cervical tenderness or high-risk mechanism suggesting fracture or dislocation
Severe or thunderclap headache or focal signs suggesting arterial dissection
Reduced consciousness or features of significant head injury
reference.prognosis: Most people recover within weeks to a few months, but a substantial minority develop chronic neck pain and disability, more likely with high initial pain, neurological signs, and psychological distress.
pitfalls: Failing to clear the cervical spine and missing a fracture, dislocation, or cord injury
Prescribing a soft collar and prolonged rest, which worsens outcomes
Overlooking associated concussion or arterial dissection
Not addressing psychosocial factors that predict chronicity
references: Apley & Solomon's System of Orthopaedics and Fractures
management: First exclude cervical fracture, dislocation or cord and nerve-root injury using a validated rule such as the Canadian C-spine rule, imaging with CT or MRI where indicated
Reassure and educate the patient, emphasising the generally favourable natural history
Encourage early return to normal activity and active mobilisation rather than a soft collar or prolonged rest
Provide simple analgesia such as paracetamol and non-steroidal anti-inflammatory drugs for pain relief
Refer for physiotherapy with an active, graded exercise programme
Identify psychosocial risk factors such as high initial pain and distress that predict chronicity, and address them early
Refer persistent whiplash-associated disorder to a multidisciplinary pain service, and escalate urgently for evolving neurological deficit or suspected arterial dissection
